title: The usual trade-off
text:
The usual trade-off
Strided Conv2d and pooling
• Pros: more layers “see” a larger part of the image; cheaper than full
resolution everywhere; hierarchical features.
• Con: spatial resolution shrinks: small objects and fine boundaries get
harder to localize in the deepest maps.
What we often want in dense prediction (segmentation, depth, etc.)
• Keep full (or near-full) spatial size at some stage and let each pixel “see”
a large context to classify it (car vs road vs sky).
• Idea: spread the kernel out so each step skips pixels—dilation / atrous
convolution.

title: 1D picture: where the kernel touches the input
text:
1D picture: where the kernel touches the input
Standard (dilation d = 1), kernel size k = 3 at one position
At one output location, we weight three consecutive input samples: indices
t, t+1, t+2.
Dilation d = 2 (same nominal k = 3)
We take three taps but spaced by d along the input: t, t+d, t+2d.
So
the span along the input axis is larger than a dense 3-tap, without
introducing more than k multiply-adds.
Mental model
Dilation = “inject zeros between kernel elements” then run an ordinary k-tap;
implementations fuse this, but the field of view grows with d.

title: Effective (spatial) size of a kernel (one axis)
text:
Effective (spatial) size of a kernel (one axis)
For each spatial axis, with kernel size k and dilation d (PyTorch: dilation
in {1, 2, . . . }; default 1 is standard conv):
keff = (k −1) d + 1
That is the length one filter “covers” at one position when we step through
the input.

title: Compare with striding and pooling (loose)
text:
Compare with striding and pooling (loose)
With s > 1 in Conv2d (stride)
Subsamples the output grid: you lose some spatial resolution in that layer.
Dilation > 1 with s = 1
The output grid (with suitable padding) can have the same H×W as a
standard d=1 layer; you do not subsample the grid—you space out the
weights in the field of view.
With pooling
Pooling still shrinks the map. Dilated convs are a different design axis: they
expand who talks to whom on a (often) fixed grid.

title: Numeric check: one axis
text:
Numeric check: one axis
Settings (PyTorch–style)
Hin = 7, k = 3, s = 1, p = 1, compare d = 1 vs d = 2.
Results
d = 1: Hout = (7+2−1(3−1)−1)+1 = 7.
d = 2: Hout = (7+2−2(3−1)−1)+1 = 5.
Larger d shrinks H with the same (k, p) unless you increase p to compensate
(e.g. “same”-style padding design).
In networks
In segmentation blocks, practitioners often set padding and/or crop so that a
stack of dilated convs preserves H×W where intended (DeepLab-style
resampling).

title: Larger field of view without a deeper stride ladder
text:
Larger field of view without a deeper stride ladder
Idea (qualitative)
Stacking L conv layers, each with dilation, grows the region of the input that
influences a pixel, roughly in a way that involves k and {d(1), . . . d(L)} (and s
if s > 1 in some layer), without necessarily halving the map at every level.
With DeepLab, PSPNet, U-Net+ASPP, etc.
• ASPP: in parallel, the same H×W feature map is convolved with
different d (e.g. 1, 6, 12, 18) to capture multi-scale context; outputs are
fused.
• Motivation: different object sizes need different “diameters” of context
on one grid.

title: The “gridding” issue
text:
The “gridding” issue
Intuition
If you stack layers with the same dilation, or with poorly chosen d sequences,
some input pixels may fall into gaps (never or rarely touched) when you
follow high-level feature paths—periodic holes in the induced sampling
pattern of the first layer.
In practice
• Vary d across the stack, use mixed d in one block (ASPP), or combine
with non-dilated paths / skip features.
• Deeper work on hybrid dilation: e.g. HDC (used in some segmentation
stacks) to mitigate gridding (paper-level detail, optional further reading).

title: Dilated Conv2d vs transposed (link to the other
text:
Dilated Conv2d vs transposed (link to the other
deck)
Dilated (this deck)
Typically keeps resolution (or controlled change via padding), grows context
on the same grid. Used at the end of encoders (context head) in many seg.
models.
Transposed (03-Conv2d-Transposed)
Increases H, W in the decoder. Complementary, not a substitute: many
pipelines = encoder + (optional) atrous head + (optional) upsample
(transposed / bilinear / combined).

title: Recap
text:
Recap
Core
• Dilated Conv2d = same nominal k×k template, but taps on the input
are spaced by d ⇒wider context without a smaller grid (when s=1 and
p is set).
• Shape: Hout = ⌊(Hin + 2p −d(k −1) −1)/s + 1⌋per axis; effective
span (k−1)d + 1 when you reason about the field of view.
• Multi-scale: parallel branches (ASPP) with different d; gridding: a
known stack-design issue, mitigated by mixed dilations and fusion.
• Pairs with transposed / upsampling decoders: dilated = context,
transposed = resolution.

title: Summary
text:
Summary
To remember
• A standard tool in semantic segmentation (e.g. DeepLab) for context
at full (or high) resolution.
• Parameter name: dilation in PyTorch; dilation rate in Keras;
always verify (Hout, Wout).
• Not the same as transposed conv: dilated = “holes in the kernel”,
transposed = “enlarge the feature map in the forward pass.”
